Overview

A seven-night small-group birthday escape designed to mix iconic Spain with relaxed luxury. Madrid brings the birthday energy, Seville adds history and Game of Thrones scenery, and Barcelona closes the trip with art, architecture and a stylish farewell.

Madrid = Birthday & Nightlife · Seville = Culture & GOT · Barcelona = Art & Finale

MADRID

March 26–29 · 3 Nights · The Birthday City

Madrid is Spain's energetic capital: grand boulevards, royal architecture, excellent food, serious nightlife and a polished big-city feel. It is sophisticated without being stuffy, making it the perfect place to start the trip and celebrate Nik's 40th. This leg is about easing into Spain, enjoying the city and giving the birthday night the space it deserves.

Hotel Recommendation: Dear Hotel Madrid
A modern 4-star boutique hotel on Gran Vía near Plaza de España. The appeal is the location: central, walkable and easy for first-time visitors, with a rooftop restaurant/bar and skyline views. It gives the group a stylish "budget-luxury" stay without paying full five-star prices.
Planning estimate $225–$325 per room/night
Rooms 4 rooms · double occupancy
Upgrade option The Principal Madrid Hotel — refined 5-star boutique on Gran Vía with rooftop cocktails
Secondary option Hotel URSO — intimate 5-star boutique in a 1915 palace between Chamberí and Chueca with a full spa

Day 2 — Saturday, March 27: NIK'S 40TH BIRTHDAY 🎉

📍 Madrid · The Main Event · Grown & Sexy

Schedule

Dining
TATEL Madrid — upscale Spanish/Mediterranean with a glamorous, social atmosphere. Expect elevated Spanish dishes, steaks, seafood, cocktails and wine. Target €75–125+ per person. Reservation target: 8:30–9:00 PM.

Alternative: Sobrino de Botín — the world's oldest restaurant (est. 1725), famous for roast suckling pig and lamb. A historic splurge near Plaza Mayor.

Michelin-Starred Birthday Dinner Options (most to least expensive, all fit the Grown & Sexy vibe):

  1. DiverXO — 3 Michelin Stars · Chef Dabiz Muñoz · €250–350+ pp (~$290–$405+ USD)
    Avant-garde tasting menus in a theatrical, maximalist dining room. Ranked #4 in the World's 50 Best. This is the ultimate splurge — bold, creative and unforgettable. Dress code matches the energy: come dressed to impress.

  2. Smoked Room — 2 Michelin Stars · Chef Dani García · €200–280 pp (~$230–$325 USD)
    A 14-seat speakeasy hidden inside Leña Madrid at the Hyatt Regency. Fire, smoke and Japanese-inspired haute cuisine. Intimate, exclusive and undeniably sexy — perfect for a small birthday group that wants a once-in-a-lifetime meal.

  3. Coque — 2 Michelin Stars · Chef Mario Sandoval · €180–250 pp (~$210–$290 USD)
    A multi-stage culinary journey across 1,100 m² — cocktail lounge, wine cellar, open kitchen, then the dining room. Elegant, theatrical and social. The experience format is made for a celebration.

  4. Ramón Freixa Madrid — 2 Michelin Stars · Chef Ramón Freixa · €150–220 pp (~$175–$255 USD)
    Luxurious Mediterranean fine dining inside Hotel Único in the Salamanca district. Glass-fronted terrace, private dining room, impeccable service. Refined and glamorous without being overly formal.

  5. Clos Madrid — 1 Michelin Star · Sommelier Marcos Granda · €120–180 pp (~$140–$210 USD)
    A wine-forward fine dining concept with contemporary Spanish cuisine in a sleek, modern setting. Excellent wine pairings and a sophisticated atmosphere — elegant without the price tag of a 2- or 3-star.

USD estimates based on ~€1 = $1.15. Actual rates will vary at time of travel.

Madrid — Where the Locals Go (Safe & Off the Tourist Trail)

Skip the crowded plazas and eat, drink, and explore where Madrileños actually hang out:

  • Malasaña — Madrid's coolest neighborhood. Vintage shops, specialty coffee, dive bars next to matcha cafés. Walk past Plaza del Dos de Mayo deeper into Plaza de las Comendadoras — it goes from trendy to genuinely local. Great for recovery day wandering.
  • La Latina — Sunday tapas crawl along Cava Baja is a local tradition. Dozens of small bars, no menus in English, incredible food. Also the best Sunday afternoon/evening energy in Madrid.
  • Chamberí — Elegant, quiet, residential. Old-school vermouth bars, neighborhood bakeries, zero tourists. The 11 PM terrace vibe here is authentic Madrid.
  • Barrio de las Letras (Huertas) — The literary quarter. Wine bars, jazz, live music, and great late-night tapas. Less hectic than Sol but still walkable from the hotel.
  • Mercado de la Paz (Salamanca) — A local market hidden behind fancy residential blocks. Butchers, fishmongers, anchovy counters, jamón slicers. Not a tourist market.

All of these neighborhoods are safe, walkable, and 10–15 minutes from Gran Vía by foot or metro.

SEVILLE

March 29–30 · 1 Night · Culture + Game of Thrones

Seville feels completely different from Madrid. This is the Spain of orange trees, tiled courtyards, narrow lanes, flamenco, tapas and Moorish architecture. The pace is warmer and more intimate, which makes it a great reset after the birthday weekend. It also delivers the trip's Game of Thrones moment: the Royal Alcázar portrayed the Water Gardens of Dorne.

Hotel Recommendation: H10 Casa de la Plata
A stylish 4-star hotel in Seville's historic center with a contemporary take on a traditional Andalusian home, including an interior courtyard and rooftop terrace. It offers the right mix of charm, convenience and value for a small group.
Planning estimate $175–$275 per room/night (1 night)
Rooms 4 rooms · double occupancy

Secondary option Hotel Casa 1800 Sevilla — charming 19th-century mansion in Santa Cruz with Cathedral views from the rooftop

How We're Doing the GOT Tour

The Royal Alcázar served as the Water Gardens of Dorne in Game of Thrones (Season 5+). Key filming locations inside the palace include:
- Patio de las Doncellas — the grand courtyard where the Martells gathered
- Salón de Embajadores — the throne room used for Dornish palace interiors
- Alcázar Gardens — the lush Water Gardens where Myrcella Baratheon stayed
- Baños de Doña María de Padilla — underground baths featured in multiple scenes

We'll book a guided GOT-themed tour with skip-the-line entry so we walk straight in and a licensed guide points out every filming location with scene breakdowns. Here are the booking options:

Seville — Where the Locals Go (Safe & Off the Tourist Trail)

Since we only have one night, here are spots to hit if you have free time before dinner:

  • Triana — Cross the Triana Bridge and you're in a completely different Seville. Working-class neighborhood known for ceramics, flamenco roots, and family-run tapas bars along Calle Betis (riverside). Safe, vibrant, zero tourists on weekday evenings.
  • Alameda de Hércules — A wide boulevard lined with local bars, live music spots, and outdoor terraces. This is where young Sevillanos go at night. Chill, artsy, inexpensive.
  • Mercado de Feria (Thursdays) — Antiques and flea market on Calle Feria that locals have browsed for decades. If our timing works, worth a walk-through.
  • Bar Condendê at Mercado de Feria — A hidden tapas gem barely any visitors know about. Locals-only energy.
  • La Taberna (Calle Gamazo) — Tiny, no-frills tapas bar. Cheap, authentic, packed with regulars.

Triana and Alameda are both safe, walkable from Santa Cruz (15–20 min), and offer a side of Seville most tourists never see.

Barcelona — Where the Locals Go (Safe & Off the Tourist Trail)

You have a full free day here. Skip the La Rambla crowds and explore where Barcelona actually lives:

  • Gràcia — A village inside the city. Tiny plazas (Plaça del Sol, Plaça de la Vila de Gràcia) surrounded by local bars, independent shops, and zero chain restaurants. Sunday vermut (vermouth hour) here is a ritual. Safe, walkable, charming.
  • Sant Antoni — Trendy but still local. The renovated Mercat de Sant Antoni on Sundays has a legendary book/vintage market. Great brunch spots, craft coffee, and wine bars. Feels like Brooklyn but Spanish.
  • Poblenou — Barcelona's creative/tech district near the beach. Old factories turned into galleries, rooftop bars, and local seafood restaurants. Way less crowded than Barceloneta for beach time.
  • El Born — Right next to the Gothic Quarter but feels more authentic. Narrow medieval streets, independent boutiques, natural wine bars, and the stunning Basílica de Santa Maria del Mar. Great for an evening stroll + dinner.
  • Bogatell Beach — Skip Barceloneta (tourist-packed). Walk 10 minutes further to Bogatell — same Mediterranean water, way fewer people, local crowd. Beach bars (chiringuitos) are cheaper here too.
  • Can Paixano (La Xampanyeria) — Locals-only cava bar in Barceloneta. Standing room only, cheap sparkling wine and charcuterie. Loud, fun, authentic. Cash only.

Gràcia and Sant Antoni are both safe day and night, easily reached by metro (L3 Fontana for Gràcia, L2 Sant Antoni). Poblenou is a quick tram ride from the center.

Dining Guide

What Are Tapas?
Tapas are small dishes meant to be shared across the table — think appetizer-sized portions, but you order several and everyone passes them around. It's social dining at its best. Instead of one person ordering one entrée, the group picks 8–12 plates and shares everything. Expect things like croquetas (fried béchamel bites), patatas bravas (crispy potatoes with spicy sauce), jamón ibérico (thinly sliced cured ham), grilled shrimp, marinated olives, Spanish tortilla (thick potato omelet), and more. Pair with wine, sangria, or beer. There's no "wrong" way to do tapas — just keep ordering until the table is happy.

Beyond Tapas — What Else You'll Eat in Spain:
- Paella — saffron rice with seafood, chicken, or vegetables (a Valencia original, popular everywhere)
- Cochinillo / Cordero asado — roast suckling pig or lamb, slow-cooked in wood-fired ovens
- Pescado a la plancha — fresh fish grilled simply with olive oil, garlic, and lemon
- Gambas al ajillo — sizzling shrimp in garlic and olive oil
- Secreto ibérico — a prized cut of Iberian pork, grilled to perfection
- Salmorejo — chilled Andalusian tomato soup (thicker and richer than gazpacho)
- Rabo de toro — braised oxtail stew (Seville specialty)
- Churros con chocolate — fried dough with thick hot chocolate for dipping (breakfast or late-night snack)
- Pintxos — Basque-style bites served on small bread slices with toothpicks (popular in Madrid too)
- Mediterranean seafood platters — oysters, razor clams, octopus, prawns, and grilled squid

The food plan is intentionally varied. We are not doing a luxury restaurant every night. The trip mixes tapas, full sit-down dinners, brunch, traditional Andalusian food, seafood, one major birthday splurge and one elegant farewell dinner. We eat.

Tips for the Group

✈ Airfare
Book your own multi-city/open-jaw ticket — into Madrid and out of Barcelona. Everyone can choose their preferred airline, points strategy or trip extension.

🛂 Passport & Entry
Confirm your passport has sufficient validity for your travel dates. U.S. citizens do not need a visa for stays under 90 days, but ETIAS pre-authorization may be required by 2027 — check the official EU ETIAS page and Spain's entry requirements closer to departure.

💶 Currency & Exchange
Spain uses the euro (€). Cards are widely accepted, but keep a small amount of cash (€100–€150) for cafés, tips and small purchases.

  • Best option: Visit your local bank or credit union 2–3 weeks before departure to order euros. Banks typically offer better exchange rates and lower fees than airport kiosks or currency exchange shops. Call ahead — most branches need 3–5 business days to get euros in stock.
  • If the rate isn't great: Wait and withdraw euros from ATMs in Spain using a no-foreign-transaction-fee debit card (Charles Schwab, Wise, Capital One 360). Spanish ATMs offer competitive rates and you avoid markup entirely. Just decline the "conversion" option at the ATM (choose to be charged in euros, not dollars).
  • Avoid: Airport currency exchange counters (both U.S. and Spain) and tourist-area "cambio" shops — they charge 5–10% markups.
  • Monitor rates: Check the ECB exchange rate leading up to the trip. If €1 dips below $1.10, that's a good time to exchange at your bank.

🛍 VAT Refund (Tax-Free Shopping)
Spain charges 21% VAT on most purchases. As non-EU residents, you can claim a tax-free refund on goods you take home — up to 15.7% back with no minimum purchase amount. Ask for a tax-free form at the register when you buy, then validate it electronically at the DIVA kiosk in the airport before you check bags on departure day.

🍽 Dining Hours
Spain eats later than the U.S. A birthday dinner around 8:30–9:00 PM is normal, not "late."

💵 Tipping in Spain
Spain does NOT have U.S.-style tipping culture. Service charge is typically included in the bill. Here's what's appropriate:

  • Restaurants: Round up or leave 5–10% for excellent service. Not required — no one will chase you down.
  • Tapas bars: Leave small coins (€0.50–€1) on the bar or round up. Many locals leave nothing.
  • Taxis: Round up to the nearest euro. A €14.30 ride? Hand over €15.
  • Hotels: €1–€2 per bag for porters; €1–€2/day for housekeeping (optional).
  • Tour guides: €5–€10 per person for a full-day guided tour if the experience was great.
  • Bottom line: Tipping is a gesture of appreciation, not an obligation. Don't stress about it.

🌤 Weather
Late March can be cool in Madrid, milder in Seville and breezy in Barcelona. Pack layers and a light jacket.

👟 Shoes
Bring comfortable walking shoes. Historic centers, plazas and palace grounds mean a lot of steps and uneven surfaces.

🔌 Power
Spain uses European Type C/F outlets (two round prongs). Your U.S. plugs will NOT fit without an adapter. Bring a plug adapter — check whether your devices support 230V before using them (most phone/laptop chargers do; hair tools often don't).

Pick one up on Amazon before you go: European Travel Adapter on Amazon — they're $8–15 and small enough to toss in your carry-on. Buy one per person.

📱 Phones
Consider an international plan or eSIM and download offline maps before arrival.

🔒 Safety & Pickpockets
Spain is safe for tourists, but pickpockets are real — especially in Barcelona (La Rambla, the metro, Sagrada Família lines), Madrid (Gran Vía, Puerta del Sol, metro), and Seville (Cathedral area, tourist plazas). They work in teams and target distracted tourists.

How to protect yourself:
- Use a crossbody bag that zips closed — wear it in front of your body in crowded areas
- Never put your phone or wallet in a back pocket
- Keep bags zipped and held close on public transit and in crowds
- Don't leave your phone on restaurant tables (especially outdoor terraces)
- Be wary of people who "accidentally" bump into you, ask you to sign a petition, or create a distraction
- Split your cash — don't carry it all in one place. Leave extra in the hotel safe.

Bottom line: You don't need to be paranoid, just aware. Crossbody bag + front pocket phone + zipped purse = you'll be fine.

Register your trip with the U.S. Embassy through the Smart Traveler Enrollment Program (STEP) — it's free and allows the embassy to contact you in an emergency abroad.

🚆 Transportation
Madrid → Seville is best by high-speed train. Seville → Barcelona is best by air for this short itinerary.

🚗 Getting Around Each City
Spain has great rideshare and taxi options:
- Uber — Available in Madrid and Barcelona. Works just like home. Not available in Seville.
- Cabify — Spain's homegrown rideshare app. Available in all three cities (Madrid, Seville, Barcelona). Download before you go: cabify.com
- Free Now (formerly mytaxi) — Hails licensed taxis through an app. Available in all three cities: free-now.com
- Taxis — Plentiful and reasonably priced in all cities. White cars with a colored stripe. Metered, no negotiation needed.
- Metro — Madrid and Barcelona both have excellent metro systems. Cheap (~€1.50–2/ride), fast, and easy to navigate. Great for getting to/from dinner without surge pricing.

Tip: Download Cabify and Uber before the trip. For group rides (8 people), you'll likely need two cars — or use a taxi van (ask for a "monovolumen" at the taxi stand).

🎟 Reservations
Major attractions and the birthday dinner should be booked in advance. The Royal Alcázar and Sagrada Família are priority timed-entry reservations.

Packing Priorities

  • Birthday night: one Grown & Sexy look
  • Seville group-photo day: one Mediterranean Neutrals look
  • Comfortable walking shoes + one dressier shoe option
  • Light jacket, layers and sunglasses
  • Crossbody or secure day bag
  • Portable charger and EU plug adapter
  • Travel-size medications and copies of important travel information

Medications — Bring Your Own

Spain has pharmacies (farmacias, marked with a green cross) on nearly every block, but they may not carry your exact brand or dosage, and some medications that are OTC in the U.S. require a prescription in Spain. Pack these in your carry-on — not checked luggage:

  • Prescription meds — bring enough for the full trip + 2 extra days in case of delays. Keep them in the original labeled bottle.
  • Pain relief — Advil/Tylenol/ibuprofen (sold in Spain but easier to have your go-to)
  • Stomach relief — Pepto-Bismol, Imodium, antacids. New food + wine + late dinners can catch up with you.
  • Allergy meds — Benadryl, Claritin, Zyrtec (spring in Spain = pollen)
  • Cold/flu — DayQuil, NyQuil, cough drops. Planes + new environments = vulnerable immune system.
  • Motion sickness — Dramamine if you get carsick (winding roads, fast trains, flights)
  • Band-Aids & blister pads — you WILL walk 15,000+ steps/day. New shoes + cobblestones = blisters.
  • Sunscreen & lip balm with SPF — late March sun in Seville hits different
  • Any personal health items — contacts, birth control, inhaler, EpiPen, etc.

Bottom line: If you take it at home, bring it with you. Don't assume you can find it in Spain.

Travel Insurance

Phoenix Travel recommends Allianz Travel Insurance for all travelers.

Travel insurance is not included in the trip cost but is strongly encouraged. It protects your investment if you need to cancel, and covers you for medical emergencies, lost luggage, flight delays, and trip interruptions while abroad.

Why it matters:
- U.S. health insurance typically does NOT cover you in Spain
- If you get sick, injured, or need emergency medical care, you'll pay out of pocket without travel insurance
- If you need to cancel for a covered reason, insurance can reimburse your non-refundable trip payments
- Flight cancellations, delays, and lost baggage are covered

What to do:
1. Visit Allianz Travel Insurance
2. Get a quote using your trip dates (March 25 – April 1, 2027) and trip cost (~$1,350)
3. Purchase your policy as soon as you make your first payment — many plans require purchase within 14 days of your first trip deposit for full benefits

Allianz is the Phoenix Travel supported insurance agency. Purchase is optional but highly recommended.
